title: Nucleophiles
keyIdea: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor. It uses a lone pair, often with a negative charge, to attack a δ+ atom and form a new covalent bond. Common nucleophiles are OH⁻, CN⁻ (attacking through carbon), NH₃, H₂O and the hydride ion H⁻ from NaBH₄. An electrophile is the opposite: an electron-pair acceptor such as H⁺, NO₂⁺ or a polarised Br₂. Nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbon of a C–halogen bond (substitution) or of a C=O bond (addition).

kid: A nucleophile gives away a pair of electrons to make a new bond. The name means nucleus-loving: it is drawn to a positive centre.
To give a pair, it needs a lone pair. OH⁻, CN⁻ and H⁻ have one and a minus charge. NH₃ and H₂O are neutral, but N and O still have lone pairs. So a charge is not needed. A lone pair is.
Where does it attack? A halogen or an oxygen pulls electrons out of its bond to carbon. That leaves the carbon δ+. The pair goes to that δ+ carbon, never to the δ− atom.
An electrophile does the reverse. It takes a pair. H⁺ and NO₂⁺ have no pair to give. Br₂ turns δ+ at one end when it nears a C=C bond.
adult: A-level chemistry calls a nucleophile an electron-pair donor. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor. Students must know OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and H₂O as the nucleophiles that react with haloalkanes. They also meet H⁻ from NaBH₄, and CN⁻, adding to aldehydes and ketones. In each case the curly arrow starts at the lone pair and ends at the δ+ carbon.

The δ+ site comes from bond polarity. Halogens and oxygen pull electrons more than carbon does, so the carbon in C–X or C=O is δ+. With a haloalkane, the halide ion leaves: this is nucleophilic substitution. With C=O, the π bond breaks and nothing leaves: this is nucleophilic addition. With an alkene, the π bond gives the pair, so the other reagent is an electrophile.

Common mistakes: thinking a nucleophile must be negative, so missing NH₃ and H₂O. Saying cyanide attacks through N; in fact the C attacks, so the chain gains a carbon (1-bromopropane gives butanenitrile). Aiming the arrow at the δ− atom. Naming Na⁺ as the nucleophile in NaBH₄. Mixing up substitution, where something leaves, with addition, where nothing leaves.

In the lab you tap the donor atom in five species and sort eight species into donors, acceptors or neither. Then you find the δ+ target in three molecules, predict five products and name six mechanisms.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to sort OH⁻, NO₂⁺, NH₃ and Br₂ into donors and acceptors, and to explain why NH₃ counts even though it has no charge.

visual.caption: Does the nucleophile replace an atom (substitution) or add across C=O (addition)? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the donor pair, sort donors from acceptors, aim at δ+, predict products and name the mechanism.

practice.prompt: Which of these species is a nucleophile?
practice.hint: Look for a lone pair that could be donated, not for a charge.
practice.explain: NH₃ has a lone pair on N, so it can donate a pair. NO₂⁺ and H⁺ can only accept a pair: they are electrophiles.

practice.prompt: A 1-bromoalkane with {n} carbon atoms is warmed with KCN in ethanol. How many carbon atoms does the nitrile have?
practice.hint: Cyanide attacks through its carbon atom. Does that carbon join the chain?
practice.explain: CN⁻ bonds through C, so its carbon joins the chain: {n} + 1 = {=n+1} carbon atoms.

practice.prompt: In chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, which atom does OH⁻ attack?
choices: The carbon of the CH₃ group
practice.hint: Which atom is left δ+ by the polar bond?
practice.explain: Cl is more electronegative, so the carbon bonded to it is δ+. The OH⁻ lone pair attacks that carbon and Cl leaves as Cl⁻.

practice.prompt: Each water molecule has 2 lone pairs on its oxygen. How many lone pairs are there in total on {n} water molecules?
practice.hint: Multiply the lone pairs per molecule by the number of molecules.
practice.explain: 2 lone pairs × {n} molecules = {=2*n} lone pairs. Any one of them can be donated, which is why water is a weak nucleophile.

pool.prompt: Which is the best definition of a nucleophile?
pool.hint: Think about what the nucleophile does with its lone pair.
pool.explain: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a new bond. Neutral NH₃ and H₂O are nucleophiles too, so a charge is not required.

pool.prompt: Which of these species is an electrophile?
pool.hint: An electrophile accepts a pair. Which one has none to give?
pool.explain: NO₂⁺ is positive with no lone pair to donate, so it accepts a pair. CN⁻ and H₂O donate pairs.

pool.prompt: A ketone with {n} carbon atoms is reduced by NaBH₄. How many carbon atoms does the alcohol product have?
pool.hint: H⁻ adds a hydrogen, not a carbon.
pool.explain: H⁻ adds to the δ+ carbon and O gains H, so the chain is unchanged: {n} carbon atoms.

pool.prompt: {n} mol of 1-bromopropane reacts fully with excess KCN. How many moles of new C–C bonds form?
pool.hint: Each CN⁻ makes one new bond from its carbon to the δ+ carbon.
pool.explain: One new C–C bond forms per molecule, so {n} mol of new C–C bonds.

pool.prompt: Why can water act as a nucleophile?
pool.hint: A nucleophile needs something to donate.
pool.explain: The oxygen has two lone pairs it can donate. δ+ hydrogens attract pairs rather than give them.

pool.prompt: CN⁻ reacts with ethanal. What is the mechanism?
pool.hint: Does anything leave when the C=O opens?
pool.explain: CN⁻ donates a pair to the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π bond breaks. Nothing leaves, so it is nucleophilic addition.

pool.prompt: NaBH₄ reduces propanal. What is the nucleophile?
pool.hint: Which part of NaBH₄ carries the electron pair to the carbon?
pool.explain: BH₄⁻ delivers H⁻, which donates its pair to the δ+ carbon. Na⁺ is a spectator ion.

pool.prompt: In bromoethane, why does OH⁻ attack carbon rather than bromine?
choices: Br pulls electrons, leaving C δ+
pool.hint: Compare the electronegativity of C and Br.
pool.explain: Br is more electronegative, so the C–Br carbon is δ+ and attracts the lone pair. Br is δ− and leaves as Br⁻.
